Engines are a fairly simple concept. You can teach yourself using the internet of knowledge (aka jewtube and forums).

1) Fuel/air mixture goes in though the intake valves.
2) Piston compresses it
3) Explosion pushes piston back down
4) Piston goes up, pushing burnt air out of exhaust valves.

The above is the basic concept of a standard four stroke engine (what your car has). Everything is just added to make that work.

The piston pushes down on the crankshaft.
The crankshaft rotates, giving power to the flywheel.
The clutch connects the flywheel to the transmission.
The transmission spins the driveshaft.
The driveshaft spins gears in the differential.
The differential gives power to the wheels.
The wheels make the car go forward (or backwards).

K, so... here's the good news: The car probably shifts and runs better (limp mode avoided) after the tranny flush. The bad news is - it (probably) wasn't a bad TCC solenoid. Yes, that's what the OBD II scanner showed you, but all it knows is that the TCC solenoid couldn't do something it was supposed to. It doesn't know that the reason behind that is either dirty transmission fluid keeping the valve from opening/closing, or the actual TCC slipping (also due to dirty tranny fluid) when the TCC solenoid engaged. If it was the latter, you're living on borrowed time before you have to drop the tranny to replace the TCC. Then again I had a truck go for 15k miles after similar issues (I didn't replace the TCC, but flushed and flushed again) without issue, so if you got out in front of the dirty tranny fluid you could be alright. But if it's been running this way for a while, shifting harder and harder til something gave... you could be in for a BIG job and a lot of money gone or a hand-off job and even more money gone.

I was a novice mechanic myself once, and I will give you some good advice about OBD II scanners - they are telling you a symptom of a problem, and that symptom is just being reported by a module. Faulty modules are often NOT the source of the error (except maybe MAF sensors, especially if you just ran some vapor/mist through your intake that you shouldn't have). E.g. O2 sensors - yes they can go bad, but odds are if you're getting some error from an O2 sensor, it's because your intake/combustion/exhaust system isn't working right. I actually had a vacuum leak in my PCV line that was throwing an O2 sensor error on my downstream (behind cat) O2 sensor.

Also, YouTube is a Godsend to back yard mechanics. Between ChrisFix and Scotty Kilmer alone, you can get some pretty good entry-level knowledge.

But I think the best part is building your tool collection and STILL saving money by not going to a service shop. Good mechanics might save you money on 1-time jobs, but a dealer shop is definitely going to shaft you.
